source.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
source.authors: A. Jermyn; Nicholas Schiefer; Evan Hubinger

record.tranche_reason: Tests feature representation and polysemanticity in sparse-feature toy networks, but uses a different architecture and monosemanticity measurements rather than reproducing the original study's method.
record.gate_note: The text reports results on toy-network feature coding, monosemanticity, neuron count, and feature sparsity. Cited findings from other work are not recorded. Numerical traces appearing only in figures are not transcribed where the text gives only qualitative descriptions.
record.test_reason: Toy sparse-feature networks with known ground-truth features. The study measures neuron polysemanticity as width, feature density and training path vary. With k=1024 > N=512 it finds equal-loss polysemantic and monosemantic basins, which bears directly on whether capacity explains polysemanticity (V2, V3). The learned feature-direction geometry of V1 is not measured, because the d=64 bottleneck is a fixed random projection.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add three points. The authors weakly hold that polysemanticity is how models cope with too few neurons. They show it also arises at k>N depending on which minimum training finds. They interpret residual ~d polysemantic neurons as a low-rank identity adjusting confidence.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says its two-layer model is most similar to the original toy-model work, but adds a linear layer so neuron count can vary independently of feature count and input dimension. It studies monosemanticity through feature-to-neuron activations and engineered training minima.
record.method_sensitivity: Monosemanticity varies with learning rate, initial bias, bias weight-decay rate, feature frequency, neuron width, activation function, and task.
record.problems: The authors call the work preliminary and report only toy models. Direction angles are not measured. Several conclusions are qualitative or described from figures without numerical uncertainty. Engineering highly monosemantic solutions depends on training choices, especially bias initialization and weight decay; the authors also report that some sparsity settings require longer training.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Figure-only traces without textually stated numerical values are represented only by the qualitative trends the text explicitly describes.

untested.parts: All of it. The d-dim embedding is a fixed random projection, and learned feature-direction geometry, near-orthogonality and phase transitions in a bottleneck are not measured.
Whether more important features get dedicated dimensions; importance is not varied.

missing.what: Power-law feature frequencies with zero initial bias: equal-loss solutions of differing monosemanticity, with the highest LR most monosemantic. This replicates the V3 evidence of R1.
The polysemantic-neuron count tracks embedding dimension (33 at d=32, 130 at d=128) and implements a low-rank identity with singular values 0.99–1.03.
Zero-bias versus negative-bias width sweep: zero-bias models are much less monosemantic at every k, with similar loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 links were dropped: the study measures neuron-basis monosemanticity in a wide layer, not learned superposition geometry. Its smooth (not sharp) density transition is reported in R4, but in a setting different from V1's bottleneck. Its V3 'not tested' is wrong: equal-loss polysemantic basins with k=2N are direct evidence for V3. This is a preprint, with no uncertainty estimates; trends are mostly read from figures.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures feature-to-neuron activation patterns, not angles or distances between feature directions; it does not establish that shared directions are nearly orthogonal or describe their regular geometry.

The study does not directly quantify feature importance as a determinant of which features receive dedicated dimensions. It examines uniform and power-law feature frequencies, neuron width, and the effects of feature density.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from mechanisms other than capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
No LLMs or SAE/dictionary features are studied.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are studied.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron monosemanticity across learning-rate runs with zero initial mean bias.
rows.measure: Monosemantic neurons and feature-to-neuron activation patterns.
rows.value: Models achieved the same loss but had very different numbers of monosemantic neurons. In the highest-learning-rate model, 503/512 features had a single monosemantic neuron, 5 features had two, and the remaining 4 had mostly-monosemantic neurons with 0.9 < ri < 0.999.
rows.note: The authors describe different training runs as reaching different loss minima and implementing different algorithms. Feature/neuron selectivity is measured, but direction angles are not.
rows.check: Re-linked from V1/V2. With twice as many neurons as features, low-LR runs are highly polysemantic at the same loss as monosemantic runs. That is polysemanticity without capacity pressure (observed for V3), and it counts against capacity as the sole cause for V2. The 503/512 figure is from the highest-LR model only.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.1; Figures 3–4: k=1024, equal-loss solutions with markedly different monosemanticity across learning rates.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Initialized with negative mean bias and used bias weight decay during training.
rows.measure: Monosemanticity and count of positive-bias polysemantic neurons.
rows.baseline: Models trained without the negative initial mean bias had more variable monosemanticity across learning rates.
rows.value: Negative initial mean bias produced highly monosemantic solutions across the tested learning rates. Each model had exactly 65 neurons with positive biases, used as a proxy for polysemantic neurons.
rows.note: This is an engineered representation. The authors report 65 positive-bias neurons, one more than d = 64.
rows.check: Re-linked from V1/V2. Negative-bias init gives highly monosemantic solutions at comparable loss, so the polysemanticity was not required. The residual ~d polysemantic neurons (65 at d=64, 33 at d=32, 130 at d=128) implement a low-rank identity, a functional rather than capacity reason. Monosemanticity here is engineered on purpose.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.2; Figures 7, 10–11: approximately −1 initial mean bias, comparable loss, and 65 positive-bias neurons at d=64.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; nonlinear dimension k varied from 16 to 2048
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of neurons in the nonlinear layer.
rows.measure: Number of monosemantic neurons and task loss as neuron width changes.
rows.baseline: Models with fewer neurons; zero-initial-bias runs are also shown alongside negative-initial-bias runs.
rows.value: Increasing neuron count increased the number of monosemantic neurons. Loss decreased until the number of neurons exceeded the number of features, then showed sharply diminishing returns. The authors report that modestly more neurons than features can support at least one monosemantic neuron per feature.
rows.note: The study also reports that negative-bias models were slightly worse for k = 256, 384, and 512, indistinguishable in loss for k = 16–128, and better for k > 512 than zero-bias models.
rows.check: Remove V1. More neurons give more monosemantic neurons. Loss improves until k exceeds N, consistent with the capacity account. The authors call this view weakly held. With negative bias, many neurons are monosemantic even at k<N at no loss cost.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.4; Figures 15–17: increasing width increases monosemantic-neuron count; loss improvements diminish beyond k=N=512.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 1024
rows.operation_detail: Measured monosemanticity while varying feature frequency.
rows.measure: Fraction of monosemantic neurons and ratio of monosemantic neurons to features.
rows.value: Monosemanticity peaks around feature frequency 2^-5 ≈ 0.03. As frequency increases, models become more polysemantic; the transition begins around Nε = d/4, and by Nε ≈ 2d there are almost no monosemantic neurons left. The authors report a smooth transition, not a sharp phase transition.
rows.note: The paper relates the change near Nε = d to a change from exact to approximate recovery in its compressed-sensing task.
rows.check: Remove V1: this is neuron-basis polysemanticity in a wide layer, not learned superposition geometry. The value is fine. Polysemanticity rises as Nε approaches d, explained by compressed-sensing limits of the d-dim bottleneck. The transition is smooth, not sharp.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.5; Figures 18–20: peak near ε=2^-5≈0.03; increasing polysemanticity thereafter; almost no monosemantic neurons at Nε≈2d.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 1024
rows.operation_detail: Compared monosemanticity across feature sparsities and bias weight-decay rates.
rows.baseline: Higher feature frequencies and faster weight decay rates.
rows.value: At very high sparsity, monosemanticity fell with the tested setup because the initial negative bias decayed before the model learned most features. Slower weight decay produced more monosemanticity in this regime; the authors expect further slowing and longer training could produce uniformly high fractions.
rows.note: The authors attribute this low-frequency result to the training protocol and slower learning, rather than concluding that sparse features cannot be represented monosemantically.
rows.check: The drop at very high sparsity is attributed to the bias-decay training protocol, not to representation capacity. This is an artefact of the engineering method.

rows.subject: random re-projector toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 1024
rows.operation_detail: Used a negative initial mean bias and varied learning rate.
rows.measure: Number of monosemantic neurons relative to features.
rows.value: The models achieved roughly one monosemantic neuron per feature across a range of learning rates.
rows.note: The result is described qualitatively; no per-model numerical values are given in the text.
rows.check: Engineered monosemanticity in the re-projector. No zero-bias comparison is reported, so it does not show polysemanticity arising otherwise. It is the study's own method result.

rows.subject: absolute value toy network
rows.size_stated: N = 512 features; d = 64 input dimensions; k = 2048
rows.operation_detail: Varied learning rate and weight decay in training.
rows.baseline: Less-monosemantic solutions in the same task.
rows.value: The more monosemantic models achieved lower loss. A negative initial bias alone was insufficient to robustly produce highly monosemantic models; slower weight decay produced more monosemantic solutions.
rows.note: The authors suggest the task takes longer to learn, so the bias must remain negative for longer for training to reach a monosemantic basin.
rows.check: Re-linked from V1. With k=2048 (4N), largely polysemantic basins occur even with bias -1; they have higher loss. Polysemanticity here arises from training dynamics, not neuron scarcity. The 'partial' state reflected the engineering success, not the claim.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3; Figures 22–23; Appendix A, Table 1: absolute-value models with k=2048; more monosemantic solutions have lower loss; negative bias alone is insufficient.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy network
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature-output curves from models trained at two feature frequencies.

conditions.value: single active feature, amplitude varied from 0 to 1

rows.measure: Output amplitude and activation thresholds of monosemantic neurons.
rows.value: At feature frequency 1/256, the monosemantic output became nonzero at input amplitude ≈ 0.3 versus ≈ 0.4 in the higher-frequency model; high-amplitude outputs were closer to the ground truth, and the second kink for features represented by two monosemantic neurons moved from ≈ 0.8 to ≈ 0.6.
rows.note: The authors interpret these changes as greater confidence that features are real, because interference is less frequent at lower feature frequency.
rows.check: Mechanistic output curves of monosemantic neurons versus feature frequency. These do not measure superposition or polysemanticity rates.

relationships.condition: Feature decoder, width sweep and feature-density sweep
relationships.reason: Monosemantic neurons increase with width, and loss saturates past k=N (R3). Polysemanticity sets in as features per sample approach d (R4).
relationships.display_finding: The number of monosemantic neurons grew with width, and loss saturated once neurons k exceeded features N. Polysemanticity set in as the number of features per sample approached the dimension d.

relationships.condition: Feature decoder and absolute-value tasks with k>N
relationships.reason: Equal-loss polysemantic minima exist at k=1024 (R1) and can be avoided via bias init (R2). Polysemantic basins also occur at k=2048 (R7). Residual ~d polysemantic neurons serve a low-rank identity (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Polysemantic minima with the same loss as monosemantic ones existed at k=1024, and a bias initialization let training avoid them, though roughly d polysemantic neurons remained, serving a low-rank identity. Polysemantic basins also occurred at k=2048.

tranche.reason: The additional linear layer permits independent variation of nonlinear-layer width; feature selectivity and training-path comparisons address the capacity explanation through a different experimental setup.

source_check.notes: The pack's code=n conflicts with Appendix A's reported GitHub implementation. Spare capacity refers to nonlinear-layer neurons; the compressed input remains lower-dimensional than the feature space, and these experiments do not establish learned superposition geometry.

statements.correction: Section 2: active feature amplitudes are uniform on [0,1]. Sections 4.1.1 and 4.3: polysemantic solutions occur with sufficient nonlinear-layer width; monosemanticity depends on learning rate, bias initialization and bias decay.
statements.problem: The causal qualification is supported, but the cited results from this study concern continuous-valued feature-decoder and absolute-value tasks, not Boolean tasks.

statements.correction: Appendix A: an implementation of the model and training process is available on GitHub.
statements.problem: The experimental claims are supported, but the assertion that code is not reported contradicts Appendix A.

statements.correction: Author list and reference EHO+22b: Nicholas Schiefer coauthors this study and Toy Models of Superposition. Section 4.1.1: sufficient nonlinear-layer width k=1024>N=512; compressed input dimension remains d=64.
statements.problem: The initialization-related result is supported, but this study's author overlap can be identified from the supplied text.
